newsitem.title: UK: Cocoa nations head toward deadlock on reserve fund.
newsitem.headline: Cocoa nations head toward deadlock on reserve fund.

text.p: Cocoa nations on Friday showed no sign of breaking an impasse over a decision to set up a reserve fund with the proceeds of buffer stock sales.

A council session of the International Cocoa Organization (ICCO) this week saw producer and consumer camps shifting ground on the issue of creating a fund for a future liquidation of the ICCO, but with little scope for agreement.
While a surge in cocoa prices injected a dose of optimism to cocoa talks, delegates could not settle their differences on a tiny slice of a forecast $300 million buffer stock sales.
Producers on Thursday set aside their initial reservations and tabled a new proposal that the fund be created from the buffer stock money, to which they are mostly entitled.

But they insisted that the ICCO first reimburses members with the last 1.5 tranches of the buffer stock revenues according to plan. These, from the sale of the remaining 51,000 tonnes of cocoa out of a total 250,000 tonnes will be paid out in September and next March.
This remains the sticking point as consumers want to create a pool of money from the buffer stock revenues irrespective of members' contributions.
"Producers say "that's the offer on the table" and consumers say "we can't accept it"," said one consumer spokesman.

Brazil, which was the biggest contributor to buffer stocks gathered in the 1970s to boost cocoa prices, has been the main opponent to moves spearheaded by consumer countries to create the reserve fund using the revenues.
Producers have contributed 80 percent of buffer stocks that the ICCO has been liquidating since 1993 after the system proved ineffective as a support mechanism to sliding prices.

But if producers succumb to consumers' suggestion, they will foot most of the reserve fund bill. Discussions have not started yet on the size of the fund but some countries say a compromise could be found around 3-4 million sterling.
Brazil said it had already allocated its share of an estimated $99 million buffer stock money that remains to be paid to the fight against witch's broom.
"If there is no solidarity in the producer camp we can't agree to anything," said Hermann Schloeder, head of the German delegation.

Some producers, including Brazil, are also opposed to consumers' ideas of using the reserve fund to generate interest income to bridge the ICCO budget shortfall when buffer stock sales are completed in March 1998. These have contributed to 40 percent of ICCO's administrative costs.

Producers have given some ground from their original proposal that the liquidation should be funded separately from members' contributions -- an idea that angered consumers who are reluctant to see a spike in annual contributions.
Brazil is also concerned about the legal aspect of channelling the buffer stock money to an entirely different purpose.
The issue has been on the ICCO agenda since December. A concensus is needed for an agreement.
